notes.front: What is a segmented circle?
notes.back: A ground marker system at airports without an operating tower that gives traffic pattern information.
notes.explanation: It gathers the wind, landing direction and pattern indicators in one place that pilots in the air and on the ground can see.
notes.example: Like a road sign for the circuit at an airfield with no tower, but laid out as a ring on the ground.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-3-4, “Visual Indicators at Airports Without an Operating Control Tower”
notes.evidence: a segmented circle visual indicator system, if installed, is designed to provide traffic pattern information

notes.front: What is a wind sock?
notes.back: A wind direction indicator near the runway; its large end points into the wind.
notes.explanation: Knowing where the wind comes from tells you which runway and pattern to use when nobody on the radio tells you.
notes.example: Like a flag streaming from a pole, but a tapering tube whose open large end faces the wind.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-3-4, “Visual Indicators at Airports Without an Operating Control Tower”
notes.evidence: The large end of the wind cone/wind sock points into the wind

notes.front: What is a tetrahedron at an airport?
notes.back: A landing direction indicator; its small end points in the direction of landing.
notes.explanation: The Aeronautical Information Manual warns against using it for anything but landing direction, including wind direction; it may be lit for night operations.
notes.example: Like an arrow laid on the airfield, but a three-sided solid that may sit in the middle of a segmented circle.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-3-4, “Visual Indicators at Airports Without an Operating Control Tower”
notes.evidence: The small end of the tetrahedron points in the direction of landing.

notes.front: What is a displaced threshold?
notes.back: A threshold located at a point on the runway other than its designated beginning.
notes.explanation: Moving the threshold down the runway shortens the length you may use for landing.
notes.example: Like a finish line painted part way along a track, but marking where landing may begin.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 2-3-3, “Runway Markings”
notes.evidence: A displaced threshold is a threshold located at a point on the runway other than the designated beginning of the runway.

notes.front: What is a hold short line?
notes.back: The runway holding position marking you must stop before when told to “hold short”, with no part of the aircraft beyond it.
notes.explanation: It is the physical limit of a hold short instruction, so it keeps aircraft out of the runway environment.
notes.example: Like the stop line at a road junction, but painted across a taxiway before a runway.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 2-3-5, “Holding Position Markings”
notes.evidence: the pilot MUST STOP so that no part of the aircraft extends beyond the runway holding position marking

notes.front: What is an ILS critical area?
notes.back: An area around an instrument landing system that must be kept clear of obstacles to protect the quality of its signal.
notes.explanation: Arriving instrument aircraft may depend on a good signal in poor weather, so ATC sometimes holds taxiing aircraft short of it.
notes.example: Like a no-parking zone in front of a fire station, but protecting a radio signal instead of a doorway.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 14, “Holding Position Signs and Markings for an Instrument Landing System (ILS) Critical Area”, p. 14-12
notes.evidence: ILSs have critical areas that must be kept clear of all

notes.front: What is a runway incursion?
notes.back: Any occurrence in the runway environment involving an aircraft, vehicle, person or object on the ground that creates a collision hazard.
notes.explanation: The definition also covers a loss of required separation with an aircraft taking off or landing, not only actual collisions.
notes.example: Like a car crossing a level crossing as the train approaches, but on an airport runway.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 14, “Runway Incursion Avoidance”, p. 14-31
notes.evidence: A runway incursion is “any occurrence in the airport runway

notes.front: What are land and hold short operations (LAHSO)?
notes.back: An ATC procedure in which a landing aircraft holds short of an intersecting runway, taxiway or other designated point.
notes.explanation: They let a controller run takeoffs and landings on intersecting runways at the same time, increasing airport capacity.
notes.example: Like stopping before a busy crossroads on a long road, but on a landing roll.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-3-11, “Pilot Responsibilities When Conducting Land and Hold Short Operations (LAHSO)”
notes.evidence: These operations include landing and holding short of an intersecting runway, an intersecting taxiway, or some other designated point on a runway

notes.front: What is pilot-controlled lighting (PCL)?
notes.back: Airport lighting that, at selected non-towered airports, the pilot turns on by clicking the radio microphone on a set frequency.
notes.explanation: At airports without a tower the lights are not always run by a person, so the pilot can switch them on from the air.
notes.example: Like a light with a clap switch, but worked by pressing the transmit button.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 14, “Control of Airport Lighting”, p. 14-18
notes.evidence: At selected nontowered airports, the pilot may control the

notes.front: What are runway status lights (RWSL)?
notes.back: An automatic system of red warning lights that shows when it is unsafe to enter, cross, take off from or land on a runway.
notes.explanation: The system was introduced to reduce runway incursions, which develop quickly with little time to correct them.
notes.example: Like a red traffic light at a level crossing that comes on by itself, but it never gives you permission to go.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 14, “New Lighting Technologies”, p. 14-19
notes.evidence: is designed to provide a direct indication to you that it is unsafe

notes.front: What are runway end identifier lights (REIL)?
notes.back: A pair of synchronised flashing lights, one on each side of the runway threshold.
notes.explanation: They give rapid and positive identification of the approach end of a particular runway.
notes.example: Like the flashing lights either side of a level crossing, but marking where a runway begins.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 14, “Runway End Identifier Lights (REIL)”, p. 14-17
notes.evidence: of a pair of synchronized flashing lights located laterally

notes.front: What is a transponder code?
notes.back: The four-digit number set on the transponder, each digit from 0 to 7, giving 4,096 possible codes.
notes.explanation: Controllers either use a standard code or assign one, and ask for it with the word “squawk”.
notes.example: Like a phone extension number, but dialled into the aircraft for radar to see.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 14, “Transponder”, p. 14-25
notes.evidence: A transponder code consists of four numbers from 0 to 7

notes.front: What is a readback?
notes.back: Repeating key parts of an ATC clearance or instruction back to the controller so both can check it.
notes.explanation: Reading back the numbers is a double check that catches a number that was misheard or given wrongly.
notes.example: Like repeating a phone number back to the caller, but for altitudes, headings and runways.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-4-7, “Pilot Responsibility upon Clearance Issuance”
notes.evidence: The read back of the “numbers" serves as a double check between pilots and controllers

notes.front: What is ground control?
notes.back: The tower position, on its own frequency, that issues taxi information and clearances to aircraft and vehicles on the airport.
notes.explanation: Separate ground frequencies keep taxi traffic off the tower (local control) frequency and prevent congestion.
notes.example: Like a car park attendant directing cars to the exit, but for aircraft moving on the airport.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-3-14, “Communications”
notes.evidence: Ground control frequencies are provided to eliminate frequency congestion on the tower (local control) frequency

notes.front: What is a flight service station (FSS)?
notes.back: An air traffic facility that gives pilot briefings, processes flight plans and provides search and rescue services, among others.
notes.explanation: It also relays ATC clearances, processes Notices to Airmen and broadcasts aviation weather.
notes.example: Like a travel information desk, but for pilots planning and flying a trip.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-1-3, “Flight Service Stations”
notes.evidence: Flight Service Stations (FSSs) are air traffic facilities that provide pilot briefings, flight plan processing, en route flight advisories, search and rescue services

notes.front: What is the upwind leg of a traffic pattern?
notes.back: A flight path that begins after departure and continues straight ahead along the extended runway centreline.
notes.explanation: It extends the departure path and is used by controllers for separation, spacing or sequencing instructions.
notes.example: Like carrying straight on after a motorway slip road, but climbing out along the runway line.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-3-2, “Airports with an Operating Control Tower”
notes.evidence: Upwind leg. A flight path that begins after departure and continues straight ahead along the extended runway centerline.

notes.front: What is the crosswind leg of a traffic pattern?
notes.back: A flight path at right angles to the landing runway off its takeoff end.
notes.explanation: It lies off the takeoff end of the runway, whereas the base leg lies off the approach end.
notes.example: Like the short end of a running track, but beyond the departure end of the runway.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-3-2, “Airports with an Operating Control Tower”
notes.evidence: Crosswind leg. A flight path at right angles to the landing runway off its takeoff end.

notes.front: What is the downwind leg of a traffic pattern?
notes.back: A flight path parallel to the landing runway, in the opposite direction to landing.
notes.explanation: Pattern altitude is held on this leg until abeam the approach end of the landing runway.
notes.example: Like the back straight of a racetrack, running beside but away from the finish.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-3-2, “Airports with an Operating Control Tower”
notes.evidence: Downwind leg. A flight path parallel to the landing runway in the opposite direction of landing.

notes.front: What is the base leg of a traffic pattern?
notes.back: A flight path at right angles to the landing runway off its approach end, from downwind to the extended centreline.
notes.explanation: It ends where the final approach begins, at the extended runway centreline.
notes.example: Like the last bend before the home straight, but crossing in front of the runway.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-3-2, “Airports with an Operating Control Tower”
notes.evidence: Base leg. A flight path at right angles to the landing runway off its approach end

notes.front: What is the final approach of a traffic pattern?
notes.back: A flight path in the direction of landing along the extended runway centreline, from the base leg to the runway.
notes.explanation: It is the only leg flown straight towards the runway in the landing direction.
notes.example: Like the home straight of a racetrack, ending at the runway.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-3-2, “Airports with an Operating Control Tower”
notes.evidence: Final approach. A flight path in the direction of landing along the extended runway centerline from the base leg to the runway.

notes.front: Besides wind direction, what can a wind sock show you?
notes.back: Wind strength and gustiness: it extends straighter in strong wind and moves back and forth in gusts.
notes.explanation: That is why the handbook calls it a good source of information for estimating wind velocity and gust factor.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 14, “Wind Direction Indicators”, p. 14-20
notes.evidence: out straighter in strong winds and tends to move back and forth

notes.front: Which part of a segmented circle shows the direction of turns when the pattern differs from the normal left-hand one?
notes.back: The traffic pattern indicators, arranged in pairs with the landing strip indicators.
notes.explanation: They exist for runways where the standard left-hand pattern does not apply.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-3-4, “Visual Indicators at Airports Without an Operating Control Tower”
notes.evidence: used to indicate the direction of turns when there is a variation from the normal left traffic pattern

notes.front: At an airport without an operating control tower in Class G airspace, which way must an airplane turn when approaching to land?
notes.back: To the left, unless approved light signals or visual markings show right turns.
notes.explanation: Only approved light signals or visual markings can change the direction to right turns.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.126(b)(1), Operating on or in the vicinity of an airport in Class G airspace
notes.evidence: must make all turns to the left unless the airport displays approved light signals or visual markings indicating that turns should be made to the right
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: At what height above ground level is it recommended that propeller-driven aircraft enter the traffic pattern?
notes.back: 1,000 feet above ground level, unless another pattern altitude is published.
notes.explanation: A common pattern altitude keeps aircraft at a predictable height; a published one in the Chart Supplement takes precedence.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-3-3, “Traffic Patterns”
notes.evidence: Propeller-driven aircraft enter the traffic pattern at 1,000 feet above ground level (AGL).

notes.front: Where and how does the FAA key to traffic pattern operations say to enter the pattern?
notes.back: In level flight, abeam the midpoint of the runway, at pattern altitude.
notes.explanation: The same key then has you hold pattern altitude on downwind until abeam the approach end.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-3-3, “Traffic Patterns”
notes.evidence: Enter pattern in level flight, abeam the midpoint of the runway, at pattern altitude.

notes.front: How should you leave the traffic pattern after takeoff?
notes.back: Continue straight out, or turn 45° in the pattern’s direction beyond the runway end after reaching pattern altitude.
notes.explanation: The turn is to the left in a left-hand pattern and to the right in a right-hand one.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-3-3, “Traffic Patterns”
notes.evidence: If departing the traffic pattern, continue straight out, or exit with a 45 degree turn

notes.front: What is the FAA’s position on VFR straight-in approaches at non-towered airports?
notes.back: It discourages them; if you fly one, announce about 8 to 10 miles out, and you have no priority over pattern traffic.
notes.explanation: The FAA links straight-in approaches with an increased risk of mid-air collision.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-1-9, “Traffic Advisory Practices at Airports Without Operating Control Towers”
notes.evidence: The FAA discourages VFR straight-in approaches to landings due to the increased risk of a mid-air collision.

notes.front: Which aircraft has the right of way over all other air traffic?
notes.back: An aircraft in distress.
notes.explanation: The regulation puts distress above every other right-of-way rule.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.113(c), Right-of-way rules: Except water operations
notes.evidence: An aircraft in distress has the right-of-way over all other air traffic.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Two airplanes converge at about the same altitude, not head-on. Which has the right of way?
notes.back: The aircraft to the other’s right.
notes.explanation: Knowing which one is on the right settles who gives way, as long as both are the same category.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.113(d), Right-of-way rules: Except water operations
notes.evidence: the aircraft to the other's right has the right-of-way
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Converging with aircraft of other categories, which category has the right of way over all of them?
notes.back: A balloon.
notes.explanation: Balloons come first in the converging order because the rule lists them above every other category.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.113(d)(1), Right-of-way rules: Except water operations
notes.evidence: A balloon has the right-of-way over any other category of aircraft
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: When a glider and a powered aircraft converge, which has the right of way?
notes.back: The glider.
notes.explanation: The converging rules give an unpowered glider priority over powered aircraft.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.113(d)(2), Right-of-way rules: Except water operations
notes.evidence: A glider has the right-of-way over powered aircraft.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Two aircraft approach each other head-on. What must each pilot do?
notes.back: Alter course to the right.
notes.explanation: The rule applies whenever aircraft approach each other head-on, or nearly so.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.113(e), Right-of-way rules: Except water operations
notes.evidence: each pilot of each aircraft shall alter course to the right
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: When one aircraft overtakes another, who has the right of way and how does the overtaking aircraft pass?
notes.back: The aircraft being overtaken; the overtaking aircraft alters course to the right to pass well clear.
notes.explanation: The overtaking pilot must also pass well clear.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.113(f), Right-of-way rules: Except water operations
notes.evidence: Each aircraft that is being overtaken has the right-of-way and each pilot of an overtaking aircraft shall alter course to the right to pass well clear.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Which aircraft have the right of way over other aircraft in flight or on the surface near an airport?
notes.back: Aircraft on final approach to land or landing.
notes.explanation: They must not use this rule to force off the runway an aircraft that has landed and is clearing it.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.113(g), Right-of-way rules: Except water operations
notes.evidence: Aircraft, while on final approach to land or while landing, have the right-of-way over other aircraft in flight or operating on the surface
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: When two aircraft approach an airport to land, which has the right of way?
notes.back: The aircraft at the lower altitude.
notes.explanation: It still must not use this to cut in front of, or overtake, an aircraft on final approach.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.113(g), Right-of-way rules: Except water operations
notes.evidence: the aircraft at the lower altitude has the right-of-way
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What may the runway behind a displaced threshold be used for?
notes.back: Takeoffs in either direction and landings from the opposite direction.
notes.explanation: Only landing towards the displaced threshold from its own end is excluded; the pavement is still runway.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 2-3-3, “Runway Markings”
notes.evidence: The portion of runway behind a displaced threshold is available for takeoffs in either direction and landings from the opposite direction.

notes.front: When a runway threshold is relocated (for example, for construction), what may the closed portion be used for?
notes.back: Taxiing only; it is not available for takeoff or landing.
notes.explanation: Relocation closes part of the approach end, and it also shortens the runway available to aircraft using it in the opposite direction.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 14, “Relocated Runway Threshold”, p. 14-5
notes.evidence: the closed portion of the runway is not available for use by aircraft for takeoff or

notes.front: What do yellow chevrons on pavement aligned with a runway mean?
notes.back: The area is unusable for landing, takeoff and taxiing.
notes.explanation: They mark pavement aligned with the runway, such as a blast pad, that is not for aircraft use.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 2-3-3, “Runway Markings”
notes.evidence: These markings are used to show pavement areas aligned with the runway that are unusable for landing, takeoff, and taxiing.

notes.front: On a runway holding position marking, which side are the solid lines on?
notes.back: Always on the side where the aircraft must hold.
notes.explanation: Approaching a runway you meet the solid lines first, so you stop before them.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 2-3-5, “Holding Position Markings”
notes.evidence: The solid lines are always on the side where the aircraft must hold.

notes.front: When exiting a runway, when are you clear of it, and do you need a clearance to cross the holding position marking?
notes.back: Clear once the whole aircraft has crossed both the dashed and solid lines; no ATC clearance is needed.
notes.explanation: From the runway side you meet the dashed lines first, and crossing outward removes you from the runway.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 14, “Runway Holding Position Marking”, p. 14-8
notes.evidence: An ATC clearance is not needed to cross this marking when

notes.front: What does a runway holding position sign look like?
notes.back: White characters outlined in black on a red background.
notes.explanation: The sign is an airport version of a stop sign, collocated with the painted holding position markings.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 14, “Runway Holding Position Sign”, p. 14-7
notes.evidence: The sign has white characters outlined in black on a red background.

notes.front: What do mandatory instruction signs look like, and what do they denote?
notes.back: A red background with white inscription; an entrance to a runway or critical area, or a prohibited area.
notes.explanation: Their colours match the runway holding position sign, marking places you may not pass without clearance.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 2-3-8, “Mandatory Instruction Signs”
notes.evidence: These signs have a red background with a white inscription

notes.front: What does a taxiway location sign look like?
notes.back: A black background with a yellow inscription and yellow border, showing the taxiway you are on.
notes.explanation: Its inscription is the designation of the taxiway you are on, so it confirms your position rather than showing you a route.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 2-3-9, “Location Signs”
notes.evidence: This sign has a black background with a yellow inscription and yellow border

notes.front: What does a direction sign show?
notes.back: Yellow background, black inscription: the intersecting taxiways leading out of an intersection, each with an arrow.
notes.explanation: Direction signs are normally on the left before the intersection, so you can plan the turn.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 2-3-10, “Direction Signs”
notes.evidence: Direction signs have a yellow background with a black inscription.

notes.front: What does a destination sign show?
notes.back: Yellow background, black inscription and an arrow: the taxi route to a destination such as a runway or terminal.
notes.explanation: Destination signs always carry an arrow showing the direction of the route.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 2-3-11, “Destination Signs”
notes.evidence: Destination signs always have an arrow showing the direction of the taxi route to the destination

notes.front: What kind of information do yellow-and-black information signs give?
notes.back: Areas that cannot be seen from the control tower, radio frequencies and noise abatement procedures, among others.
notes.explanation: The airport operator decides where they are needed.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 2-3-12, “Information Signs”
notes.evidence: areas that cannot be seen from the control tower, applicable radio frequencies, and noise abatement procedures

notes.front: What does a runway distance remaining sign show?
notes.back: On a black background, a white number: the landing runway remaining, in thousands of feet.
notes.explanation: The last sign, showing “1”, is at least 950 feet from the runway end.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 2-3-13, “Runway Distance Remaining Signs”
notes.evidence: The number on the signs indicates the distance (in thousands of feet) of landing runway remaining.

notes.front: On what principle does a VASI work?
notes.back: Colour difference: each light unit projects white in the upper part of its beam and red in the lower part.
notes.explanation: Which colours you see from each bar therefore depends on whether you are above, on or below the glidepath.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 14, “Visual Approach Slope Indicator (VASI)”, p. 14-16
notes.evidence: The basic principle of the VASI is that of color differentiation between red and white.

notes.front: How does a PAPI differ in layout from a VASI?
notes.back: Its lights are in a single row, normally on the left side of the runway.
notes.explanation: It uses lights similar to the VASI but arranged in one row rather than in bars.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 14, “Other Glidepath Systems”, p. 14-16
notes.evidence: except they are installed in a single row

notes.front: What colours does a tri-colour visual approach slope indicator show below, on and above the glidepath?
notes.back: Below: red. On: green. Above: amber.
notes.explanation: It is a single light unit projecting three colours along the approach path.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 14, “Other Glidepath Systems”, p. 14-17
notes.evidence: indicated by red, on the glidepath is indicated by green

notes.front: What colour are runway edge lights, and where do they change colour on an instrument runway?
notes.back: White; on instrument runways, amber on the last 2,000 feet or half the runway, whichever is less.
notes.explanation: The lights marking the end of the runway are red.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 14, “Runway Edge Lights”, p. 14-18
notes.evidence: on instrument runways where amber lights are used on the

notes.front: What colour are taxiway edge lights and taxiway centreline lights?
notes.back: Edge lights are blue; centreline lights, where installed, are green.
notes.explanation: At many airports ATC can adjust the edge lights’ intensity when needed or when a pilot asks.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 14, “Taxiway Lights”, p. 14-19
notes.evidence: Omnidirectional taxiway lights outline the edges of the

notes.front: With radio-controlled runway lighting, how do you select the highest intensity?
notes.back: Key the microphone 7 times within 5 seconds.
notes.explanation: Fewer clicks select lower intensities: 5 for medium or lower, 3 for the lowest.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 14, “Control of Airport Lighting”, p. 14-19
notes.evidence: 7 times within 5 seconds

notes.front: Do runway status lights ever give you clearance to enter a runway or take off?
notes.back: No; they show runway status only.
notes.explanation: Clearance still comes from ATC, while the red lights add a warning when the runway is unsafe.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 14, “New Lighting Technologies”, p. 14-19
notes.evidence: they do not indicate clearance to enter a runway

notes.front: How do you tell the controller you have listened to the ATIS?
notes.back: On initial contact, repeat the broadcast’s alphabetical code word, for example “information Sierra”.
notes.explanation: The controller can then skip the items in the broadcast if they are current.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-1-13, “Automatic Terminal Information Service (ATIS)”
notes.evidence: Pilots should notify controllers on initial contact that they have received the ATIS broadcast by repeating the alphabetical code word appended to the broadcast.

notes.front: What comes first in an initial radio call, and what comes second?
notes.back: First the name of the facility you are calling, then your full aircraft identification.
notes.explanation: Next come your position if on the surface and your request, so the controller knows who is calling and where.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-2-3, “Contact Procedures”
notes.evidence: Name of the facility being called;

notes.front: You hear nothing on the radio for a long time. What equipment checks should you make?
notes.back: Check your volume, recheck your frequency, and make sure your microphone is not stuck transmitting.
notes.explanation: A stuck microphone can block a frequency for long periods.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-2-2, “Radio Technique”
notes.evidence: Check your volume, recheck your frequency, and make sure that your microphone is not stuck in the transmit position.

notes.front: At a non-towered airport, when should inbound and departing pilots be on the CTAF?
notes.back: Inbound: from 10 miles out to landing. Departing: from start-up until 10 miles away.
notes.explanation: Everyone within that radius is then on the same frequency to exchange traffic information.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-1-9, “Traffic Advisory Practices at Airports Without Operating Control Towers”
notes.evidence: Pilots of inbound traffic should monitor and communicate as appropriate on the designated CTAF from 10 miles to landing.

notes.front: May you say “traffic in the area, please advise” on the CTAF?
notes.back: No; it is not a recognised self-announce phrase and should not be used.
notes.explanation: Self-announcing means stating your own position and intentions, not asking others for theirs.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-1-9, “Traffic Advisory Practices at Airports Without Operating Control Towers”
notes.evidence: is not a recognized Self-Announce Position and/or Intention phrase and should not be used under any condition

notes.front: Where there is no tower, flight service station or UNICOM, which frequency do you use to self-announce?
notes.back: MULTICOM, 122.9 MHz.
notes.explanation: Such airports are identified in aeronautical information publications.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-1-9, “Traffic Advisory Practices at Airports Without Operating Control Towers”
notes.evidence: Where there is no tower, FSS, or UNICOM station on the airport, use MULTICOM frequency 122.9 for self-announce procedures.

notes.front: Where can you find the CTAF for an airport?
notes.back: In the Chart Supplement (and on instrument charts), or by asking any flight service station.
notes.explanation: Selecting the right common frequency is the key to communicating at a non-towered airport.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-1-9, “Traffic Advisory Practices at Airports Without Operating Control Towers”
notes.evidence: The CTAF frequency for a particular airport or area is contained in the Chart Supplement U.S.

notes.front: To operate to an airport with an operational control tower, by when must two-way radio communications be established?
notes.back: Before 4 nautical miles from the airport, up to and including 2,500 feet above ground level.
notes.explanation: The rule makes two-way contact with the tower a condition of flying to, from, through or on the airport.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.126(d), Operating on or in the vicinity of an airport in Class G airspace
notes.evidence: Communications must be established prior to 4 nautical miles from the airport, up to and including 2,500 feet AGL.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: After landing at a towered airport, when do you change from the tower to the ground frequency?
notes.back: Only when the controller tells you to.
notes.explanation: Staying on the tower frequency until told to change keeps you reachable by the controller who is handling the runway you have just left.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-3-14, “Communications”
notes.evidence: A pilot who has just landed should not change from the tower frequency to the ground control frequency until directed to do so by the controller.

notes.front: What must you include in every readback and acknowledgement?
notes.back: Your aircraft identification.
notes.explanation: It lets the controller confirm the right aircraft got the instruction, which matters more when similar call signs share a frequency.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-4-7, “Pilot Responsibility upon Clearance Issuance”
notes.evidence: Include the aircraft identification in all readbacks and acknowledgments.

notes.front: When given taxi instructions, what should you always read back?
notes.back: The runway assignment, any clearance to enter a runway, and any instruction to hold short or line up and wait.
notes.explanation: Controllers must ask for a readback of a hold short assignment if you do not give one.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-3-18, “Taxiing”
notes.evidence: When taxi instructions are received from the controller, pilots should always read back:

notes.front: Which instruction must ATC obtain a readback of from the pilot?
notes.back: Every runway hold short instruction.
notes.explanation: Because the instruction keeps you off a runway, controllers must ask for the readback if you do not give it.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-3-18, “Taxiing”
notes.evidence: ATC is required to obtain a readback from the pilot of all runway hold short instructions.

notes.front: Once you have an ATC clearance, when may you deviate from it?
notes.back: Only with an amended clearance, in an emergency, or to follow a collision avoidance system resolution advisory.
notes.explanation: A pilot who is unsure of a clearance must immediately ask ATC to clarify it.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.123(a), Compliance with ATC clearances and instructions
notes.evidence: no pilot in command may deviate from that clearance unless an amended clearance is obtained, an emergency exists
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: If you cannot safely comply with an ATC instruction, what should you do?
notes.back: Tell ATC immediately, using the word “unable”.
notes.explanation: The final decision to act rests with you, and there is nothing wrong with declining an unsafe instruction.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 14, “ATC Instructions”, p. 14-33
notes.evidence: If you cannot safely comply with any of ATC’s instructions

notes.front: Does a clearance to taxi to your departure runway let you cross other runways on the way?
notes.back: No; ATC issues an explicit clearance for every runway crossing.
notes.explanation: It does not even let you enter or cross the departure runway itself.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-3-18, “Taxiing”
notes.evidence: A clearance must be obtained prior to crossing any runway. ATC will issue an explicit clearance for all runway crossings.

notes.front: At a towered airport, when may you cross a runway hold marking?
notes.back: Only with explicit ATC instructions to cross, take off from or line up and wait on that runway.
notes.explanation: The handbook lists crossing a hold marking without clearance as a pilot deviation that can lead to a runway incursion.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 14, “ATC Instructions—“Hold Short””, p. 14-33
notes.evidence: runway hold markings should never be crossed without explicit ATC instructions

notes.front: At a non-towered airport, when may you taxi onto or across a runway?
notes.back: Only when the runway is clear and no aircraft are on final approach; look both ways.
notes.explanation: The handbook adds: use extreme caution and always look both ways.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 14, “Runway Holding Position Marking”, p. 14-8
notes.evidence: you may taxi onto or across the runway

notes.front: Does “line up and wait” clear you for takeoff?
notes.back: No; it only clears you to enter the runway and hold in position for takeoff.
notes.explanation: ATC uses it when a takeoff clearance cannot be issued immediately.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 14, “ATC Instructions—“Line Up and Wait” (LUAW)”, p. 14-34
notes.evidence: An ATC instruction to “line up and wait” is not a clearance

notes.front: What are two of the three areas that investigations found contribute to runway incursions?
notes.back: Failure to comply with ATC instructions; lack of airport familiarity (also nonconformance with procedures).
notes.explanation: The handbook calls clear, concise pilot/controller communication paramount to safe surface operations.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 14, “Causal Factors of Runway Incursions”, p. 14-32
notes.evidence: Failure to comply with ATC instructions

notes.front: What are two factors that increase the risk of runway confusion and a wrong-runway departure?
notes.back: Airport complexity; close proximity of runway thresholds (also joint use of a runway as a taxiway).
notes.explanation: Runway confusion is a kind of runway incursion that you usually do not notice until after it happens.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 14, “Causal Factors of Runway Confusion”, p. 14-32
notes.evidence: Close proximity of runway thresholds

notes.front: After landing, when is your aircraft considered clear of the runway?
notes.back: When all parts are past the runway edge and nothing restricts its onward movement beyond the runway holding position markings.
notes.explanation: Unless ATC says otherwise, you are still expected to taxi beyond the holding position markings and then hold, so that the aircraft is well away from the runway.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-3-21, “Exiting the Runway After Landing”
notes.evidence: An aircraft is considered clear of the runway when all parts of the aircraft are past the runway edge and there are no restrictions to its continued movement beyond the runway holding position markings.

notes.front: When should checklists be done during taxi?
notes.back: With the aircraft stopped.
notes.explanation: Taxi needs your whole attention outside, “heads up”, with no non-essential activity.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 14, “Causal Factors of Runway Incursions”, p. 14-32
notes.evidence: All checklists should be completed while

notes.front: What control positions does the handbook give for taxiing a nosewheel airplane in a quartering headwind and in a quartering tailwind?
notes.back: Headwind: upwind aileron up, elevator neutral. Tailwind: elevator down, upwind aileron down.
notes.explanation: Each position reduces the wind’s tendency to lift the upwind wing or get under the tail.
notes.source: FAA, Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 2, “Taxiing”, p. 2-19
notes.evidence: these control positions reduce the tendency of the wind to get under the tail and the wing

image.alt: Two top views of a nosewheel airplane. Left: wind blowing from ahead and to the left, labelled quartering headwind, with the note upwind aileron up and, for nosewheel types, elevator neutral. Right: wind blowing from behind and to the left, labelled quartering tailwind, with the note elevator down and upwind aileron down.
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from FAA, Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 2, Figure 2-15

notes.front: When must aircraft position lights be on?
notes.back: From sunset to sunrise, on the surface and in flight.
notes.explanation: Anti-collision lights, by contrast, are required day and night.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-3-24, “Use of Aircraft Lights”
notes.evidence: Aircraft position lights are required to be lighted on aircraft operated on the surface and in flight from sunset to sunrise.

notes.front: When must an anti-collision light system be operated, and when may it be turned off?
notes.back: In all operations, day and night; the pilot in command may turn it off when its light would be a hazard.
notes.explanation: For example, in some adverse weather its reflections could be a hazard to safety.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-3-24, “Use of Aircraft Lights”
notes.evidence: aircraft equipped with an anti-collision light system are required to operate that light system during all types of operations (day and night)

notes.front: What does the table of ATC light signals in the regulations set out?
notes.back: Six signals, each with one meaning for aircraft on the surface and another for aircraft in flight.
notes.explanation: The same colour means different things on the ground and in the air, so you need both columns.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.125, ATC light signals
notes.evidence: ATC light signals have the meaning shown in the following table:
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

image.alt: A table of six light signals. Steady green: cleared for takeoff on the surface, cleared to land in flight. Flashing green: cleared to taxi; return for landing, to be followed by steady green. Steady red: stop; give way to other aircraft and continue circling. Flashing red: taxi clear of runway in use; airport unsafe, do not land. Flashing white: return to starting point on airport; not applicable in flight. Alternating red and green: exercise extreme caution in both cases.
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from 14 CFR § 91.125

notes.front: What does a steady green light signal mean to an aircraft on the ground?
notes.back: Cleared for takeoff.
notes.explanation: On the ground, steady green is the go signal for departure.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.125, ATC light signals
notes.evidence: Steady green Cleared for takeoff
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What does a steady green light signal mean to an aircraft in flight?
notes.back: Cleared to land.
notes.explanation: In the air, steady green is the final permission to complete the landing.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.125, ATC light signals
notes.evidence: Cleared for takeoff Cleared to land.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What does a flashing green light signal mean to an aircraft on the ground?
notes.back: Cleared to taxi.
notes.explanation: Flashing green lets you move on the ground, but not onto the runway for takeoff.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.125, ATC light signals
notes.evidence: Flashing green Cleared to taxi
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What does a flashing green light signal mean to an aircraft in flight?
notes.back: Return for landing (to be followed by steady green at the proper time).
notes.explanation: It is not yet a landing clearance; wait for the steady green.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.125, ATC light signals
notes.evidence: Return for landing (to be followed by steady green at proper time).
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What does a steady red light signal mean to an aircraft on the ground?
notes.back: Stop.
notes.explanation: On the ground, steady red is a simple stop.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.125, ATC light signals
notes.evidence: Steady red Stop Give way to other aircraft
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What does a steady red light signal mean to an aircraft in flight?
notes.back: Give way to other aircraft and continue circling.
notes.explanation: On the ground the same steady red simply means stop.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.125, ATC light signals
notes.evidence: Give way to other aircraft and continue circling.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What does a flashing red light signal mean to an aircraft on the ground?
notes.back: Taxi clear of the runway in use.
notes.explanation: It tells you to get off the runway, not simply to stop.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.125, ATC light signals
notes.evidence: Flashing red Taxi clear of runway in use
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What does a flashing red light signal mean to an aircraft in flight?
notes.back: Airport unsafe; do not land.
notes.explanation: You should look for somewhere else to land.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.125, ATC light signals
notes.evidence: Airport unsafe—do not land.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What does a flashing white light signal mean to an aircraft on the ground?
notes.back: Return to your starting point on the airport.
notes.explanation: It has no meaning for aircraft in flight.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.125, ATC light signals
notes.evidence: Flashing white Return to starting point on airport
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: What does an alternating red and green light signal mean?
notes.back: Exercise extreme caution, both on the ground and in flight.
notes.explanation: It is a general warning with the same meaning in every situation.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.125, ATC light signals
notes.evidence: Alternating red and green Exercise extreme caution
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Arriving at a towered airport with a failed receiver, what do you do first?
notes.back: Stay outside or above the Class D surface area until you know the direction and flow of traffic.
notes.explanation: Then advise the tower of type, position, altitude and intention to land, and ask to be controlled by light signals.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-2-13, “Communications with Tower when Aircraft Transmitter or Receiver or Both are Inoperative”
notes.evidence: remain outside or above the Class D surface area until the direction and flow of traffic has been determined

notes.front: With a failed transmitter, how do you acknowledge tower transmissions in flight by day and by night?
notes.back: By day, rock your wings; at night, blink the landing or navigation lights.
notes.explanation: You can still hear the tower on its frequency, so you only need a visible way to reply.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-2-13, “Communications with Tower when Aircraft Transmitter or Receiver or Both are Inoperative”
notes.evidence: During hours of daylight, acknowledge tower transmissions or light signals by rocking your wings.

notes.front: If your radio fails in flight under VFR, under what conditions may you land at a towered airport?
notes.back: Weather at or above basic VFR minimums, visual contact with the tower, and a clearance to land.
notes.explanation: The regulation lets you complete the landing by light signals in place of radio.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.126(d), Operating on or in the vicinity of an airport in Class G airspace
notes.evidence: visual contact with the tower is maintained, and a clearance to land is received
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Flying VFR, what transponder code do you set unless ATC tells you otherwise?
notes.back: 1200, whatever your altitude.
notes.explanation: It is the standard VFR code; ATC assigns another code when it needs to identify you.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-1-20, “Transponder and ADS-B Out Operation”
notes.evidence: adjust transponder/ADS-B to reply on Mode 3/A Code 1200 regardless of altitude

notes.front: In a distress or urgency situation, which transponder code alerts ATC radar?
notes.back: 7700 (emergency), with altitude reporting.
notes.explanation: It normally triggers an alarm at all radar control positions.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 6-2-2, “Transponder Emergency Operation”
notes.evidence: Radar facilities are equipped so that Code 7700 normally triggers an alarm or special indicator at all control positions.

notes.front: Which transponder code is decoded as the hijack code?
notes.explanation: Because it triggers special alarms, you must never pass through it by accident when changing codes.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-1-20, “Transponder and ADS-B Out Operation”
notes.evidence: Only nondiscrete Code 7500 will be decoded as the hijack code.

notes.front: When changing transponder codes, which codes should you avoid passing through?
notes.explanation: Even a moment on them causes false alarms at automated ground facilities.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-1-20, “Transponder and ADS-B Out Operation”
notes.evidence: pilots should avoid inadvertent selection of Codes 7500, 7600 or 7700 thereby causing momentary false alarms

notes.front: Does radar navigation assistance let you break a regulation or hand safety to the controller?
notes.back: No; it is advisory, and flying the aircraft safely remains your job.
notes.explanation: Keep controllers told of the weather so you are not vectored into instrument conditions.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-1-17, “Radar Assistance to VFR Aircraft”
notes.evidence: the job of flying the aircraft safely, remains with the pilot

notes.front: At an uncontrolled airport with ASOS/AWOS, who has the more current weather, the pilot or a distant controller?
notes.back: The pilot; controllers rely on the pilot to find the current weather from the automated station.
notes.explanation: The automated broadcast updates every minute, while the controller may be miles away.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-3-27, “Operations at Uncontrolled Airports With Automated Surface Observing System (ASOS)/Automated Weather Observing System (AWOS)”
notes.evidence: Controllers will rely on the pilot to determine the current airport weather from the ASOS/AWOS.

notes.front: Who decides whether to accept a LAHSO clearance?
notes.back: The pilot in command, who has final authority to accept or decline it.
notes.explanation: Declining is expected if the pilot judges it would compromise safety.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-3-11, “Pilot Responsibilities When Conducting Land and Hold Short Operations (LAHSO)”
notes.evidence: The pilot-in-command has the final authority to accept or decline any land and hold short clearance.

notes.front: May a student pilot on a solo flight accept a LAHSO clearance?
notes.back: No; LAHSO are not authorised for student pilots flying solo.
notes.explanation: The handbook lists this among its LAHSO restrictions, along with wet runways and, generally, night.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 14, “Land and Hold Short Operations (LAHSO)”, p. 14-11
notes.evidence: LAHSO are not authorized for student pilots who are performing a solo flight.

notes.front: Landing behind a larger aircraft on the same runway, how do you avoid its wake?
notes.back: Stay at or above its approach path and land beyond its touchdown point.
notes.explanation: Wingtip vortices are produced from lift-off to touchdown, so the wake lies below its path and ends where it touched down.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 14, “Vortex Avoidance Procedures”, p. 14-28
notes.evidence: land beyond its touchdown point

notes.front: In this drawing of a segmented circle, the pattern indicator at the south end of runway 36/18 has its arm pointing east. Which way do you turn when landing on runway 36?
notes.back: To the right: runway 36 has a right-hand pattern, with base and downwind east of the runway.
notes.explanation: Turns are to the left unless a traffic pattern indicator shows right turns; this indicator's arm points east, the side on which the base and downwind legs lie.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-3-4, “Visual Indicators at Airports Without an Operating Control Tower”
notes.evidence: all turns must be made to the left unless a traffic pattern indicator indicates that turns should be made to the right

image.alt: A dashed yellow circle with a wind cone at its centre. A north-south runway, 36/18, is marked by a landing strip indicator north and south of the circle. Beyond each landing strip indicator is an L-shaped traffic pattern indicator: a bar along the runway line with a short arm at its outer end pointing east.
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-3-4, and Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge, ch. 14, Figure 14-38

notes.front: At a non-towered field with runways 09 and 27, the wind sock’s large end points east and it stands out straight. Which runway do you normally land on?
notes.back: B) Runway 09
notes.choices:
A) Runway 27
B) Runway 09
C) Either: a steady wind sock gives no direction
notes.choicesExplained: A would put the wind behind you on landing. C is wrong: the large end shows where the wind comes from.
notes.explanation: The large end points into the wind, so the wind is from the east, and final approach and landing are normally made into the wind.
notes.source: FAA, Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 9, “Base Leg”, p. 9-2
notes.evidence: Since the final approach and landing are normally made into the wind

notes.front: You approach an untowered Class G airport. The chart and the ground markings show right traffic for runway 22. What must you do?
notes.back: C) Make all turns to the right for runway 22
notes.choices:
A) Make left turns; the left-hand pattern always applies
B) Choose whichever direction suits the wind
C) Make all turns to the right for runway 22
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores the exception for approved right-turn markings. B is wrong: the direction of turns is set by the rule, not by pilot preference.
notes.explanation: The left-turn rule gives way where approved markings or light signals show right turns.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.126(b)(1), Operating on or in the vicinity of an airport in Class G airspace
notes.evidence: in which case the pilot must make all turns to the right
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: You are flying parallel to runway 18, heading north, planning to land on runway 18. Which leg are you on?
notes.back: The downwind leg.
notes.explanation: Runway 18 lands southbound, so flying north beside it is parallel and opposite to the landing direction.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-3-2, “Airports with an Operating Control Tower”
notes.evidence: A flight path parallel to the landing runway in the opposite direction of landing.

notes.front: You depart runway 27 at a non-towered field with a standard left-hand pattern and want to leave the area. What is the recommended way?
notes.back: A) Climb straight out, or turn 45° left beyond the runway end after reaching pattern altitude
notes.choices:
A) Climb straight out, or turn 45° left beyond the runway end after reaching pattern altitude
B) Turn 90° right immediately after lift-off
C) Turn 45° right beyond the runway end before reaching pattern altitude
notes.choicesExplained: B turns early and against the pattern. C turns the wrong way for a left-hand pattern and too low.
notes.explanation: The recommended exit is straight out or a 45° turn in the direction of the pattern once at pattern altitude.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-3-3, “Traffic Patterns”
notes.evidence: exit with a 45 degree turn (to the left when in a left-hand traffic pattern; to the right when in a right-hand traffic pattern)

notes.front: Cruising in an airplane, you see another airplane at about your altitude converging from your left, not head-on. What should you do?
notes.back: B) Hold your course but stay vigilant; the other airplane should give way to you
notes.choices:
A) Give way, because the other aircraft is on your left
B) Hold your course but stay vigilant; the other airplane should give way to you
C) Turn left towards it to pass behind
notes.choicesExplained: A reverses the rule. C turns towards the traffic; the rule gives you the right of way, and see-and-avoid still applies.
notes.explanation: Same-category aircraft converging give way to the one on the right, and you are on its right.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.113(d), Right-of-way rules: Except water operations
notes.evidence: the aircraft to the other's right has the right-of-way
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: You are on downwind at pattern altitude and see an airplane lower than you on a long final to the same runway. What do you do?
notes.back: C) Give way to it and fit in behind
notes.choices:
A) Descend quickly and turn in ahead of it
B) Continue your normal pattern; it must extend its final
C) Give way to it and fit in behind
notes.choicesExplained: A cuts in front of an aircraft on final, which the rule forbids. B ignores its right of way.
notes.explanation: An aircraft on final, and the lower of two aircraft approaching to land, has the right of way.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.113(g), Right-of-way rules: Except water operations
notes.evidence: the aircraft at the lower altitude has the right-of-way
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: A runway’s centreline has a magnetic direction of 047° in the direction of landing. What number is painted on its approach end?
notes.explanation: The number is the whole number nearest one-tenth of the magnetic azimuth.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 14, “Runway Designation Marking”, p. 14-8
notes.evidence: Runway numbers and letters are determined from the

notes.front: Runway 17 has a displaced threshold. You are departing on runway 17. Where may you begin your takeoff roll?
notes.back: B) From the beginning of the pavement, behind the displaced threshold
notes.choices:
A) Only from the displaced threshold bar
B) From the beginning of the pavement, behind the displaced threshold
C) Nowhere on runway 17 until the displacement is removed
notes.choicesExplained: A wastes usable runway: the restriction is on landing, not takeoff. C is wrong: the runway remains open.
notes.explanation: The portion behind a displaced threshold is available for takeoffs in either direction.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 2-3-3, “Runway Markings”
notes.evidence: available for takeoffs in either direction

notes.front: Before runway 32 is a paved area marked with large yellow chevrons. May you use it to start your takeoff roll?
notes.back: C) No: chevron areas are unusable for takeoff, landing and taxiing
notes.choices:
A) Yes, as with a displaced threshold
B) Yes, but only for taxiing onto the runway
C) No: chevron areas are unusable for takeoff, landing and taxiing
notes.choicesExplained: A confuses chevrons with the white arrows of a displaced threshold. B is wrong: taxiing is also excluded.
notes.explanation: The chevrons mean the pavement is not for any aircraft movement.

notes.front: Ahead of you on a taxiway is a red sign with white “4-22” on it. What type of sign is it, and what does it mean?
notes.back: A mandatory instruction sign: a runway holding position for runway 4-22; do not pass without clearance at a towered airport.
notes.explanation: Red with white inscription marks an entrance to a runway.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 2-3-8, “Mandatory Instruction Signs”
notes.evidence: An entrance to a runway or critical area

notes.front: On a runway with a typical 3° PAPI, your approach angle is 3.6°. Which indication does the PAPI give: high, slightly high, on glidepath, slightly low or low?
notes.back: High (more than 3.5°).

notes.front: Before calling a towered airport you tune the ATIS and hear “information Bravo”. What should your first call include?
notes.back: C) Your call sign, position and request, and “with Bravo”
notes.explanation: Saying you have Bravo lets the controller confirm you have the current weather without repeating it.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 14, “Automated Terminal Information Service (ATIS)”, p. 14-5
notes.evidence: the tower controller, state information Bravo was received.
notes.choices:
A) Your call sign only; the controller will read you the weather
B) “Have numbers”
C) Your call sign, position and request, and “with Bravo”
notes.choicesExplained: A wastes frequency time the ATIS exists to save. B confirms only wind, runway and altimeter, not the ATIS.

notes.front: You are at the south ramp and ready to taxi for a local VFR flight. Which call to ground follows the recommended format?
notes.back: B) “Springfield Ground, Cessna One Two Three Four Five, south ramp, ready to taxi, VFR local”
notes.choices:
A) “Cessna One Two Three Four Five, ready to taxi”
B) “Springfield Ground, Cessna One Two Three Four Five, south ramp, ready to taxi, VFR local”
C) “Springfield Ground, ready to taxi, any traffic please advise”
notes.choicesExplained: A omits the facility and your position. C omits your identification and position.
notes.explanation: The format is facility, full identification, position on the surface, then the request.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-2-3, “Contact Procedures”
notes.evidence: When operating on an airport surface, state your position.

notes.front: You are 10 miles south of Strawn, a non-towered airport, inbound to land on runway 17. What is the best call?
notes.back: A) “Strawn traffic, Cessna Two Three Four, ten miles south, descending through three thousand, landing runway one seven, Strawn”

A) “Strawn traffic, Cessna Two Three Four, ten miles south, descending through three thousand, landing runway one seven, Strawn”
B) “Traffic in the area, please advise”
C) “Cessna Two Three Four, landing the active”
notes.choicesExplained: B is not a recognised self-announce phrase. C omits the airport name and uses “the active” instead of the number.
notes.explanation: It names the airport at the start and end, gives position and altitude, and uses the runway number.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-1-9, “Traffic Advisory Practices at Airports Without Operating Control Towers”
notes.evidence: Strawn traffic, Apache Two Two Five Zulu, (position), (altitude), (descending) or entering downwind/base/final

notes.front: Which facility would you call for a preflight weather briefing and to file a VFR flight plan?
notes.back: B) A flight service station
notes.choices:
A) Ground control
B) A flight service station
C) The airport’s UNICOM
notes.choicesExplained: A handles taxi instructions on the airport. C is a non-government station for airport information.
notes.explanation: Pilot briefings and flight plan processing are core services of a flight service station.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-1-3, “Flight Service Stations”
notes.evidence: provide pilot briefings, flight plan processing

notes.front: Ground says: “November 477ZA, runway four, taxi via Echo, hold short of runway two five at Delta.” What is the best readback?
notes.back: A) “Runway four via Echo, hold short of runway two five at Delta, November 477ZA”
notes.choices:
A) “Runway four via Echo, hold short of runway two five at Delta, November 477ZA”
B) “Roger, November 477ZA”
C) “Wilco”
notes.choicesExplained: B and C do not read back the hold short instruction, which ATC must obtain.
notes.explanation: A full readback includes the runway, the route, the hold short instruction and your call sign.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 14, “ATC Instructions—Explicit Runway Crossing”, p. 14-34
notes.evidence: Pilot November 477ZA, Runway four via Echo, hold short of Runway two five at Delta.

notes.front: The tower tells you to extend your downwind, but ahead is a cloud you cannot fly through under VFR. What should you do?

A) Fly into the cloud; ATC instructions must be obeyed

C) Tell the tower you are unable and why, and ask for an alternative
notes.choicesExplained: A puts compliance above safety and VFR rules. B deviates without telling ATC.
notes.explanation: You must not simply deviate without telling ATC, and you should say “unable” when you cannot comply safely.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 14, “ATC Instructions”, p. 14-33
notes.evidence: There is nothing wrong with telling a controller that you are

notes.front: You were told: “Runway two seven, taxi via Alpha.” Taxiway Alpha crosses runway three one. What do you do at runway three one?
notes.back: B) Stop at its holding position and ask for a crossing clearance
notes.choices:
A) Cross after looking both ways; you are cleared to runway 27
B) Stop at its holding position and ask for a crossing clearance
C) Cross, as long as no aircraft is on final
notes.choicesExplained: A and C treat the taxi instruction as a crossing clearance, which it is not.
notes.explanation: A taxi instruction to your runway does not include crossing another; every crossing needs its own clearance.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-3-18, “Taxiing”
notes.evidence: ATC will issue an explicit clearance for all runway crossings.

notes.front: At an unfamiliar, busy towered airport, ground gives you a long taxi route you are not sure of. What is the best action?
notes.back: A) Ask for progressive taxi instructions and follow the airport diagram
notes.choices:
A) Ask for progressive taxi instructions and follow the airport diagram
B) Follow the aircraft ahead of you
C) Start taxiing and ask again if you get lost
notes.choicesExplained: B assumes the other aircraft has your clearance and route. C moves before the route is understood.
notes.explanation: Lack of airport familiarity and misunderstood instructions are major causes of runway incursions.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 14, “Causal Factors of Runway Incursions”, p. 14-32
notes.evidence: Lack of airport familiarity

notes.front: You taxi a nosewheel airplane with the wind blowing from behind you and from the left. How do you position the controls?
notes.back: B) Elevator down, left (upwind) aileron down
notes.choices:
A) Elevator up, left aileron up
B) Elevator down, left (upwind) aileron down
C) Elevator neutral, right aileron down
notes.choicesExplained: A is close to the headwind positions and lets the wind get under the tail. C puts the downwind aileron down and ignores the tail.
notes.explanation: With a quartering tailwind, both the elevator and the upwind aileron are held down.
notes.source: FAA, Airplane Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-3C), ch. 2, “Taxiing”, p. 2-19
notes.evidence: When taxiing with a quartering tailwind

notes.front: At night you are cleared to line up and wait on the runway. Which lights should you have on?
notes.back: A) All exterior lights except the landing lights
notes.choices:
A) All exterior lights except the landing lights
B) Only position lights, to avoid dazzling the tower
C) Landing lights only
notes.choicesExplained: B makes you hard to see on the runway. C omits the anti-collision and position lights and shows landing lights before takeoff clearance.
notes.explanation: All lights except landing lights make you conspicuous to ATC and aircraft on approach while you wait.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-3-24, “Use of Aircraft Lights”
notes.evidence: When entering the departure runway for takeoff or to “line up and wait,” all lights, except for landing lights, should be illuminated

notes.front: With a failed radio, you are in the pattern at a towered airport and see a flashing green light from the tower. What does it mean?
notes.back: B) Return for landing; wait for a steady green before landing
notes.choices:
A) Cleared to land
B) Return for landing; wait for a steady green before landing
C) Airport unsafe, do not land
notes.choicesExplained: A is steady green. C is flashing red.
notes.explanation: In flight, flashing green means return for landing, to be followed by steady green at the proper time.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.125, ATC light signals
notes.evidence: Return for landing (to be followed by steady green at proper time).
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Holding short of the runway with a dead radio, you see a steady green light from the tower. What may you do?
notes.back: A) Take off
notes.choices:
A) Take off
B) Taxi only
C) Return to the ramp
notes.choicesExplained: B is flashing green. C is flashing white.
notes.explanation: On the surface, steady green means cleared for takeoff.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.125, ATC light signals
notes.evidence: Steady green Cleared for takeoff
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Nearing a towered airport, you find you can hear nothing but think your transmitter works. What is the correct procedure?
notes.back: C) Stay outside the Class D area until you know the traffic flow, transmit your intentions, join the pattern and watch for light signals
notes.choices:
A) Fly straight in and land; the tower will see you
B) Circle over the tower until the radio recovers
C) Stay outside the Class D area until you know the traffic flow, transmit your intentions, join the pattern and watch for light signals
notes.choicesExplained: A enters without knowing the traffic flow or getting a signal. B does nothing to arrange a landing and may conflict with traffic.
notes.explanation: This is the receiver-inoperative procedure: determine the flow, advise the tower, then land by light signals.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-2-13, “Communications with Tower when Aircraft Transmitter or Receiver or Both are Inoperative”
notes.evidence: request that you be controlled with light signals

notes.front: ATC asks you to change from code 2700 to 7200. Which sequence is correct?
notes.choices:
A) 2700 → 2200 → 7200
B) 2700 → 7700 → 7200
C) Either; the order does not matter
notes.choicesExplained: B passes through 7700 and sets off a false emergency alarm. C ignores that risk.
notes.explanation: Changing the first digit first would pass through 7700, the emergency code.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-1-20, “Transponder and ADS-B Out Operation”
notes.evidence: switch first to 2200 then to 7200, NOT to 7700 and then 7200

notes.front: On VFR radar vectors, the heading you are given would take you into cloud. What should you do?
notes.back: B) Tell the controller about the cloud and ask for another heading
notes.choices:
A) Fly into the cloud; the vector is an instruction
B) Tell the controller about the cloud and ask for another heading
C) Say nothing and turn away
notes.choicesExplained: A breaks VFR and hands safety to the controller. C leaves the controller unaware of your position and intentions.
notes.explanation: Controllers often cannot tell whether a vector leads into instrument conditions, so you must keep them advised.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-1-17, “Radar Assistance to VFR Aircraft”
notes.evidence: pilots should keep controllers advised of the weather conditions in which they are operating and along the course ahead

notes.front: You accept “cleared to land runway 36, hold short of runway 23”. What must you do?
notes.back: A) Exit runway 36 or stop before the holding position for runway 23
notes.choices:
A) Exit runway 36 or stop before the holding position for runway 23
B) Roll through the intersection if you are slow enough
C) Land on runway 23 instead
notes.choicesExplained: B crosses the hold short point you agreed to. C lands on a runway you were not cleared for.
notes.explanation: Accepting LAHSO commits you to stopping with no part of the aircraft beyond the hold short markings.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 14, “Taxiway Markings and Signs”, p. 14-11
notes.evidence: you must either exit Runway 36 or stop at the holding position prior to Runway 23

notes.front: Flying level, you see another airplane at your altitude coming straight towards you. What do you do?
notes.back: A) Alter course to the right; the other pilot should do the same
notes.choices:
A) Alter course to the right; the other pilot should do the same
B) Alter course to the left
C) Hold course; the aircraft on the right has the right of way
notes.choicesExplained: B turns the opposite way from the rule and risks both turning into each other. C applies the converging rule, which excludes head-on encounters.
notes.explanation: Head-on, each pilot turns right, so the two aircraft turn away from each other.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.113(e), Right-of-way rules: Except water operations
notes.evidence: each pilot of each aircraft shall alter course to the right
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Planning a flight to an unfamiliar non-towered airport, where do you look up its CTAF and traffic pattern information?
notes.back: B) The Chart Supplement
