notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-1-9, “Traffic Advisory Practices at Airports Without Operating Control Towers”
notes.evidence: The CTAF frequency for a particular airport or area is contained in the Chart Supplement U.S.

notes.front: You are 6 nautical miles from a towered airport at 1,500 feet above ground level, intending to land, and have not yet called. What must you do?
notes.back: C) Establish two-way radio communication with the tower before 4 nautical miles
notes.choices:
A) Nothing yet; call when you enter the downwind leg
B) Rock your wings to get the tower’s attention
C) Establish two-way radio communication with the tower before 4 nautical miles
notes.choicesExplained: A leaves the call too late. B is a lost-communications acknowledgement, not a way to establish contact.
notes.explanation: The regulation requires two-way communication to be established before 4 nautical miles, up to 2,500 feet above ground level.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.126(d), Operating on or in the vicinity of an airport in Class G airspace
notes.evidence: no person may operate an aircraft to, from, through, or on an airport having an operational control tower unless two-way radio communications are maintained
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force

notes.front: Taxiing out in fog, you realise you have not done the before-takeoff checklist. When should you do it?
notes.back: A) After stopping clear of other traffic with the brakes set
notes.choices:
A) After stopping clear of other traffic with the brakes set
B) Now, while taxiing slowly
C) On the runway during the takeoff roll
notes.choicesExplained: B and C split your attention while the aircraft is moving, when it should be entirely on safe operation.
notes.explanation: In low visibility, checklists wait until the aircraft is stopped and the brakes are set.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-3-19, “Taxi During Low Visibility”
notes.evidence: Checklists and nonessential communication should be withheld until the aircraft is stopped and the brakes set.

notes.front: You are inbound to an uncontrolled airport in Class E airspace that has an AWOS. What should you monitor, and why?
notes.back: B) The airport weather frequency, to know whether the airspace is IFR or VFR
notes.choices:
A) Nothing: controllers will pass you the latest weather
B) The airport weather frequency, to know whether the airspace is IFR or VFR
C) The nearest flight service station only
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: controllers rely on the pilot for current weather at such airports. C misses the one-minute local weather.
notes.explanation: Pilots in Class E airspace must be alert for weather changes that alter the status of the airspace.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-3-27, “Operations at Uncontrolled Airports With Automated Surface Observing System (ASOS)/Automated Weather Observing System (AWOS)”
notes.evidence: should monitor the airport weather frequency to ascertain the status of the airspace

notes.front: You are on final behind a large jet that has just landed on the same runway. How do you plan your approach?
notes.back: C) Stay at or above its approach path and touch down beyond where it touched down
notes.choices:
A) Fly slightly below its path and land short of its touchdown point
B) Land at its exact touchdown point
C) Stay at or above its approach path and touch down beyond where it touched down
notes.choicesExplained: A flies through the sinking wake. B touches down where the wake ends, with no margin.
notes.explanation: Vortices are generated until the aircraft touches down, so the runway beyond its touchdown point is clear of them.
notes.source: FAA, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (FAA-H-8083-25C), ch. 14, “Vortex Avoidance Procedures”, p. 14-28
notes.evidence: stay at or above the larger aircraft’s approach

notes.front: The upwind leg and final approach both lie along the extended runway centreline. How do they differ?
notes.back: Upwind continues straight ahead after departure; final is flown in the landing direction from base leg to the runway.
notes.explanation: One leads away from the runway after takeoff and the other leads to it for landing.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 4-3-2, “Airports with an Operating Control Tower”
notes.evidence: A flight path in the direction of landing along the extended runway centerline from the base leg to the runway.

notes.front: How do a displaced threshold and a relocated threshold differ in what the pavement before them allows?
notes.back: Displaced: takeoffs either way and landings from the opposite end. Relocated: taxiing only.
notes.explanation: A relocated threshold closes that part of the runway, while a displaced one keeps it as runway.
notes.source: FAA, Aeronautical Information Manual, para. 2-3-3, “Runway Markings”
notes.evidence: When a threshold is relocated, it closes not only a set portion of the approach end of a runway

notes.front: How does the meaning of a flashing green light differ between an aircraft on the ground and one in flight?
notes.back: On the ground: cleared to taxi. In flight: return for landing.
notes.explanation: The regulations give each signal a separate meaning for the surface and for flight.
notes.source: 14 CFR § 91.125, ATC light signals
notes.evidence: Meaning with respect to aircraft in flight
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · FAA-S-ACS-6C and 14 CFR as in force
